how to brief a UGC creator
one_idea: A brief that lists deliverables gets you content; a brief that names one customer, one tension and one line gets you an ad, so the deliverables belong at the bottom of the page, not the top.
reader: Indian D2C founder or marketer who briefs UGC creators and freelance editors over WhatsApp, with no strategist on the team
cep: We sent the creator a brief and what came back doesn't sound like us
firsthand: Payoff's own one-page brief (the cmo-brain Gate 3 fields: the number, the customer and moment, the tension, the one line, the proof, brand codes, what it is not), cut to seven lines; plus eight years on set and in the edit: shoots go wrong on page one, and Payoff writes the one line before booking a camera.
sharp_question: How do we get a D2C founder who briefs creators with a WhatsApp list of deliverables to send a one-page story brief instead, given they have no strategist and brief several creators a month?

social.ig_caption:
Your creator isn't the problem. Your brief is.

"3 reels, 30 seconds, trending audio, show the product" is an order. It leaves the story blank, so every creator writes their own.

A brief names one customer, one moment, the tension they feel, and the one line they must remember.

The deliverables go at the bottom. Not the top.

Comment STORY and we'll send you our one-page brief.

Full post with the template on the blog (link in bio).
social.linkedin_post:
Most ad briefs I see from D2C brands are orders.

"3 reels. 30 seconds. Trending audio. Show the product. Launch Friday."

Nothing wrong with any of that. It's just the last line of a brief, sent as the whole thing.

When the story is left blank, the creator fills it in. Hire five creators and you get five brands, each saying something nice and nothing in particular.

The brief we use at Payoff fits on one page. Seven lines, in this order:

1. The number this ad should move
2. One customer, in one moment
3. The tension they feel before the product shows up
4. The one line they must remember
5. One shot that proves it
6. The brand codes that must appear in the first three seconds
7. What this ad must not say

Then the deliverables.

Eight years on set and in the edit taught me this: when a shoot goes wrong, the trouble was usually on page one. A crew can light anything. Nobody can guess the line you meant to say.

Story first. Camera second. Spend third.

The full template is on the Payoff blog.
